st:rh.riemannHypothesis: There is no hypothesis that $s$ belongs to the critical strip. For the unique character modulo $1$ the $L$-function is $\zeta$, so [Statement 2.2](pdf#theorem.2.2) excludes zeros to the right of $\tfrac12$, away from $1$. For a zero to the left, put $t=1-s$: then $\operatorname{Re}t>\tfrac12$ and $t\ne1$ since $\zeta(0)=-\tfrac12$. In the functional equation $\zeta(s)=2(2\pi)^{-t}\Gamma(t)\cos(\pi t/2)\zeta(t)$ the power, gamma and zeta factors are nonzero. Thus $t=3,5,7,\ldots$, the positive odd integers other than $1$, and $s=-2,-4,-6,\ldots$ are precisely the zeros excluded in the statement.

st:grh.LFunction_ne_zero_of_half_lt_re: The modulus is positive (`NeZero N`), and $\chi=1$ denotes the principal character modulo $N$, whose $L$-function is $\zeta(s)\prod_{p\mid N}(1-p^{-s})$ away from $1$. The factors are nonzero at $1$, so the pole occurs for the principal character of every modulus; the disjunction excludes just that case and includes $s=1$ for non-principal characters. This is a statement about the meromorphic continuation (`LFunction`), not the Dirichlet series (`LSeries`); in Lean even at a pole the former is a complex-valued function. More generally, the change of modulus from the conductor to $N$ introduces factors $1-\psi(p)p^{-s}$, where $\psi$ is the inducing primitive character; as $|\psi(p)p^{-s}|\le p^{-\operatorname{Re}s}<1$ for $\operatorname{Re}s>0$, these introduce no zeros there. Hence the primitive non-vanishing assertion `ZeroFreeAll` of [Section 3](pdf#section.3) suffices.

st:strip.LFunction_eq_zero_re: The two boundaries play different roles. At $\operatorname{Re}s=1$ non-vanishing is already included in [Statement 2.2](pdf#theorem.2.2), except at the principal pole; at $\operatorname{Re}s=0$ the extra Euler factors can vanish. For example, for the principal character modulo $2$ one has $L(s,\chi)=(1-2^{-s})\zeta(s)$ for $s\ne1$, giving a zero at $s=2\pi i/\log2$ regardless of the value of $\zeta$ there. In the left half of the open strip the factors are nonzero, so `Claim.strip` passes from a zero of $L(s,\chi)$ to one of $L(s,\psi)$ for the inducing primitive character $\psi$, then by the functional equation to a zero of $L(1-s,\psi^{-1})$. This point is to the right of $\tfrac12$ and still in the open strip, contrary to the non-vanishing theorem.

verification:64:1.LFunction_eq_zero_re_of_isPrimitive: Write $a=0$ or $1$ according as $\chi$ is even or odd. In the open strip Mathlib's completed function is $L^*(s,\chi)=\Gamma_{\mathbb R}(s+a)L(s,\chi)$, where $\Gamma_{\mathbb R}(z)=\pi^{-z/2}\Gamma(z/2)$; the gamma factor has neither a zero nor a pole there. The inverse character has the same conductor as $\chi$ and hence is primitive, so its functional equation reads $L^*(1-s,\chi^{-1})=N^{s-1/2}\varepsilon(\chi^{-1})L^*(s,\chi)$, with $\varepsilon$ the root number. Thus a zero of $L(s,\chi)$ in the strip gives a zero of $L(1-s,\chi^{-1})$. It is the inverse character that occurs in this reflection, not in general $\chi$ itself; the non-vanishing theorem applies to either character, and no change of modulus is needed in `critAll`.

overview:6:1.Formalism.HC.ZeroFreeAll: `ZeroFreeAll` is non-vanishing in $\operatorname{Re}s>\tfrac12$ for primitive characters of every conductor and either parity. Fix one such character $\psi$: the level used in the proof consists of the primitive characters inducing the powers of $\psi$, so contains $1$ and $\psi$ itself. A one-sided bound on the positively weighted sum of the real parts of their smoothed prime sums suffices: Landau on windows gives non-vanishing for every member, first to the right of $\tfrac12+C\varepsilon$ and then to the right of $\tfrac12$ since $C$ is fixed and $\varepsilon$ can be arbitrarily small. The Lean predicate has no exception at $s=1$, using Mathlib's totalised $L$-function; Statement 2.2 for arbitrary moduli expressly excludes the principal-character pole.

three-inputs.UpperTheory.Top.every_character_of_green: Let $\chi$ be a character modulo $N$, induced by a primitive character $\psi$ of conductor $N_0\mid N$. The change of modulus gives, away from the principal pole, $L(s,\chi)=L(s,\psi)\prod_{p\mid N,\,p\nmid N_0}(1-\psi(p)p^{-s})$. Every added factor is non-zero for $\operatorname{Re}s>0$, since $|\psi(p)p^{-s}|\le p^{-\operatorname{Re}s}<1$; this includes the principal character at any modulus, induced by the character modulo $1$. This is the whole extension made by `Top.imprimitive`; the same three inputs suffice, with $s=1$ excluded only for a principal character.
three-inputs.UpperTheory.Top.zero_free_all_of_green_v: Green's count of local types enters the rank estimates for the frame of period maps; together with the record `HypsAlt` it gives the lattice argument for given admissible host data. The bound for the normalised logarithmic [congruence index](pdf#subsection.8.2) $\eta_j$ contains a term depending on the cohomology lengths: `VWin` bounds their weighted sum by $\sqrt b$, where $b=\exp(x^\varepsilon)$. The same input, through `supplyChi`, supplies hosts throughout arbitrarily late windows $[Y,Y^{3/2}]$, with the level fixed but the host allowed to vary with $x$. The period estimate needs only the bound by $b$; the exponent $\tfrac12$ in $G_{\mathcal L}(x)\le x^{1/2+C\varepsilon}$ comes instead from balancing $x/m$ and $m$ at $m\approx\sqrt x$.

overview:27:1.Formalism.MainNotions.ChainTied: Fix the scale $x$. For each translate $T_2+u_0$ of the thick set there is a family of period maps $B_u:N_u\to P$, indexed by words $u$; the target $P$ is common to the words at that translate, not required to be common to different translates. The map `pt` chooses a family for each $u_0\in H$ with the same frame, the same primes $q,d$, the same number $m$ of lifts and the same sizes $a_t$, but with weights and word-indexed lattices that can vary. This permits the subsequent average over $u_0\in A_0\subset H$: after replacing the thick weights, all close to $b$, by $b$ and estimating the thin terms, orthogonality removes the characters non-trivial on $A_0$.

overview:27:2.Formalism.MainNotions.ChainTied: At a fixed translate write $\mathrm{ASK}(u_0)$ and $\mathrm{MAIN}(u_0)$ for the sums of the counts and real main terms over the top places and lifts. In combining (Gain) with (Div), $\mathrm{Fo}$ cancels exactly, and the main part $m\ell_g\sum_ta_t$ of $\mathrm{Ee}(u)$ is cancelled by the host-prime term in the lower bound for $\log T(u)$. The rank-weighted mean of $\mu(N_u)-h(u)$ over the words is then bounded below by $\mu(P)+\mathrm{Ga}(u_0)-\mathrm{MAIN}(u_0)$ less the errors, and above by $\mu(P)$ plus the frame error in (Slope). With (Loss), $\mathrm{ASK}(u_0)\le\mathrm{Ga}(u_0)+\mathrm{Lo}$, and the remaining numerical, identification and size conditions of `ChainTied`, `ch_top` gives $\mathrm{ASK}(u_0)-\mathrm{MAIN}(u_0)\le x^{C\varepsilon}\mathrm{Br}$ for each translate, at sufficiently large $x$: precisely condition (3) of [Statement 4.3](pdf#theorem.4.3).

st:landau.Deduction.zeroFree_of_rpow_window: The constant $C$, the exponents $\theta,\omega$ and the family $F$ are fixed. A zero of any member to the right of $\theta$ would force a violation of the upper bound somewhere in every sufficiently late window, not necessarily at its endpoints. It is thus enough to obtain [(4.6)](pdf#equation.4.6) at each scale of a window of admissible hosts supplied by [Statement 9.1](pdf#theorem.9.1), conditional on the cohomological bound: the auxiliary host may depend on the scale, but the function $G_{\mathcal L}$ to which the theorem is applied must be the same throughout.

level-character-weights.Formalism.HC.Level.wt: The particular coefficients here come from the count, not from Landau's theorem. In [Statement 4.3](pdf#theorem.4.3) the mean $|TT|^{-1}\sum_{t\in TT}\psi(0,t)$ is exactly $1$ for a character trivial on $H$, and for the other kept characters it is within $Mx^{-1+\varepsilon}$ of $\beta=(3o+1)^{-1}$ in the application. In an adapted host, the trivial character and the distinguished character, if present, are the only kept characters trivial on $H$. This explains the two weights in (4.2); for `Level.cyc` the distinguished character is absent and $o$ is the order of the generating character.
level-character-weights.Formalism.HC.Level.Gm: The family in Statement 4.1 is indexed by all of $\mathcal K$: `Nt` omits the trivial character only because $G=G_1$ is written separately, with weight one. For the cyclic level of order $o$, which has at most $o-1$ non-trivial members and no distinguished character, put $\beta=(3o+1)^{-1}$. Even the combined coefficient multiplying $\Lambda(n)(y/n-1)_+$ before centring is positive: $1+\beta\sum_{\psi\ne1}\operatorname{Re}\psi(n)\ge 1-\beta(o-1)>0$. This gives no sign for the centred function $G_{\mathcal L}$ and is not needed by Landau's theorem. The identity `level_family` also identifies the zero-free conditions, so the conclusion includes $\zeta$ as well as the non-trivial members.
level-character-weights.Formalism.HC.zeroFreeOn_of_levels: For a primitive character $\psi$, take the level formed by the primitive characters inducing the powers of $\psi$ (`Level.cyc ψ`). It contains $\psi$ itself. For any fixed $s$ with $\operatorname{Re}s>\tfrac12$, choose a sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$ so that $\tfrac12+C\varepsilon<\min(1,\operatorname{Re}s)$, and use the bound for this level on the corresponding windows. The windows may change with $\varepsilon$; the conclusion for the level is non-vanishing to the right of $\tfrac12$, and the covering lemma then specialises it to $\psi$.

landau-proof-idea.Deduction.landau_window: Write $g(v)=G_F(e^v)$ and $\Phi(s)=\int_0^\infty g(v)e^{-sv}\,dv$ for $\operatorname{Re}s>2$. The coefficient of $z^k$ in $\Phi(s-z)$ is $T_k(s)=\int_0^\infty g(v)v^ke^{-sv}\,dv/k!$. At a real $\sigma>2$, with $w_k(v)=v^ke^{-\sigma v}/k!$, the triangle inequality gives $|T_k(\sigma+it)|+\operatorname{Re}T_k(\sigma)\le 2\int_0^\infty\max(g(v),0)w_k(v)\,dv$. The additional real coefficient cancels the contribution of the negative part in the upper bound: one obtains an estimate at every height $t$ from an upper bound for $g$ alone, with no lower bound on the window.
landau-proof-idea.Deduction.lemmaL: The smoothing in [(4.1)](pdf#equation.4.1) gives $\int_{\log n}^\infty(e^v/n-1)e^{-sv}\,dv=n^{-s}/(s(s-1))$. For $\chi\ne1$ the resulting transform is $\bigl(-L'/L(s,\chi)+sL'/L(1,\chi)\bigr)/(s(s-1))$; the correction removes the apparent pole at $1$, and the zeta correction similarly removes its double and simple pole terms there. Taking real parts of $G_{\chi_i}(y)$ averages the transforms for $\chi_i$ and $\chi_i^{-1}$, so at a zero $\rho$ in the strip the family residue is $-S/(\rho(\rho-1))$, where $S=\sum_i a_i(m_i+m_i')/2$ and $m_i,m_i'$ are the orders of vanishing of the two functions at $\rho$. These orders are non-negative, and $S>0$ at any zero of a member: the residues cannot cancel, and at a real $0<\rho<1$ the residue is positive.

analytic:56:1.Deduction.CH.HostFactsS: Write $I_p$ for inertia at $p$: the character value at $p^i$ is the mean of $\psi$ on the coset $C_{p,i}=i\operatorname{Frob}_p+I_p$ (in additive notation), rather than its value at an arbitrary representative. For $p\in S$ the two splitting conditions put the whole coset in $\Phi$; the prime splits in the quadratic field fixed by $\Phi$, even if it ramifies in the host. At $d$, addition of $\sigma=((1,0),0)$ interchanges the two cosets of $\Phi$, so $C_{d,i}$ has exactly one element $g_i\notin\Phi$, for every $i\ge1$. The term at $d$ in (4.3) is $\log d\sum_{i\ge1}\max(a/d^i-w(\rho_{g_i}),0)$: there is no parity restriction, and the inertia average divides the usual coefficient $2\log d$ by two.

st:balance.Deduction.ch_balance: For fixed $g\notin\Phi$ put $W=w(\rho_g)$; the identity $W(a/(Wn)-1)_+=\max(a/n-W,0)$ gives the weight of the count from [(4.1)](pdf#equation.4.1). To recover the uncentred prime sum from $WG_\psi(a/W)$ one adds $a(\log a-1-\gamma-\log W)$ for $\psi=1$, and $-aL'/L(1,\psi)$ otherwise. The partner bijection averages $\log W$ over all of $\Phi$, while the mean of $\overline{\psi}(g)$ on the complementary coset is $1$ for $\psi=1$, $-1$ for $\psi=\chi_\Phi$, and zero for every other character; the latter cancellation applies to the non-trivial corrections because they no longer depend on $W$. This gives (4.4), including the plus sign of $aL'/L(1,\chi_\Phi)$, and makes MAIN independent of $t$ for fixed $a,w$. In Lean the identity holds with arbitrary `ell` in place of the logarithmic derivatives and an integer cutoff $N$ with $a/w(\rho)\le N$ for every $\rho\in\Phi$.

character-orthogonality.Deduction.ch_balance: Interchange the sums in `askExp` and fix $p^i$, with inertia group $I_p$ and coset $C_{p,i}=i\operatorname{Frob}_p+I_p$. With $\psi(p^i)$ read as the mean over this coset, orthogonality gives $|\Phi|^{-1}\sum_{\psi\in\widehat{\mathfrak G}}\overline{\psi}(g)\psi(p^i)=(2/|I_p|)\mathbf{1}_{g\in C_{p,i}}$: the factor two comes from $|\mathfrak G|=2|\Phi|$. At an unramified prime the coset is a singleton, giving the coefficient $2\log p$ after multiplication by $\Lambda(p^i)=\log p$; the condition $\chi_\Phi(\operatorname{Frob}_p)^i=-1$ selects exactly the odd powers of primes inert in the quadratic field fixed by $\Phi$; the partner weight still depends on the full Frobenius power. The series $1/p+1/p^3+\cdots$ of these reciprocal powers is the derivative gain per order at an inert prime in [Section 6.1](pdf#subsection.6.1), before the capacity and loss terms. If all weights were a common $W$, the character average on the complement would give $\mathrm{ASK}-\mathrm{MAIN}=W(G(a/W)-G_{\chi_\Phi}(a/W))$. The variable weights in Statement 4.2 instead allow other characters to occur: under its size and character hypotheses, [Statement 4.3](pdf#theorem.4.3) turns an upper bound for the sum of the real deviations at each translate into a bound for the kept sum, with an error for the omitted characters.

analytic:91:1.Deduction.CH.SizesA: For fixed $a_t$ the quantity to be approximated is $wG_\psi(a_t/w)$, not $G_\psi(a_t/w)$ alone. Multiplying (4.1) by $w$ gives the prime-sum weight $(a_t/n-w)_+$; for $\psi\ne1$ the correcting term is $a_t L'/L(1,\psi)$, independent of $w$, and for $\psi=1$ the only varying part of the correction is $a_t\log w$. The bound `LipW` thus applies without an estimate for the logarithmic derivative: on a thick place the change on replacing $w$ by $b$ is at most $3(a_t/b)(w-b)\le3(x+1)(\eta+1)$. The resulting term has the same weight at every lift, and its argument is $a_t/b$, still to be moved to $x$.

analytic:98:1.Formalism.LFunctionChainParameters.Thick: For a thin weight $w$, the inequalities $a_t\ge(x-1)b$, $w\le2b'$ and $b'X'\le xb$ give $a_t/w\ge (x-1)X'/(2x)\ge X'/3$ for $x\ge3$. It follows that $|wG_\psi(a_t/w)|\le\vartheta a_t\le\vartheta(x+1)b$: the factor $w$ cancels the denominator in the argument. This estimate is needed for every host character, not merely those in $\Psi(A_0)$, since the thin terms are removed before using orthogonality on $A_0$.

analytic:98:2.Formalism.LFunctionChainParameters.LChai: Write $f=|\Phi|=2|H|$. The outer sum in [Statement 4.2](pdf#theorem.4.2) has $f$ terms, each containing $2f$ characters; its factor $1/f$ leaves the bound $2f$ times the error for one character at one place. Thus `CostWindows` imposes $2f(x+1)b\vartheta\le b/x$ for the thin terms and $6f(x+1)(\eta+1)\le b/x$ for the change of thick weights (the latter condition is not written out above). Together they give an error at most $2b/x$ for each pair $(t,j)$, before moving the arguments $a_t/b$ to $x$.

analytic:99:1.Formalism.MainNotions.Lnk.Char_at: For a non-trivial host character $\psi$, `Char_at` identifies $\ell(\psi)$ with $L'/L(1,\chi)$ for the inducing primitive character $\chi$ (the correction in [equation (4.1)](pdf#equation.4.1)); the real part of $\ell(\chi_\Phi)$ is also the term used in MAIN. In particular the logarithmic derivatives of the kept characters of a fixed level do not change with the host. The implication from `ChThin_at` bounds $|G_\psi(y)|/y$ for every host character at $y\ge\exp(x^{\varepsilon/3})/3$; this range lies far above $x$ for large $x$. The separate implication from `ChQD_at` is for three specified quadratic characters at $x$, not a bound at $x$ for the whole kept family.

st:core.Deduction.ch_core: The conclusion concerns the signed sum $G_{\mathcal K'}$, not an estimate for each kept character: $\Sigma_{\mathcal K'}$ is the cost of the other characters that survive the translate average. In the application the latter cost is bounded using the choice of the two auxiliary primes ([Section 9.3](pdf#subsection.9.3)), whereas (3) is the count estimate supplied by the lattice argument. The threshold for $x$ in `ch_core` is chosen with $C,\varepsilon,\beta,M,K_o,C_E$ fixed, before the host is given; this is essential when the host changes with $x$. The lift bounds $x^{1/2-\varepsilon}\le m\le x^{1/2+\varepsilon/2}$ in the notation table are used only in the final size estimate, to control the opposing costs $x/m$ and $m$.

apply-count-balance.Deduction.ch_core: After the weight replacement, the term indexed by $s\in T_2$ at translate $u_0$ carries the character value $\psi(\sigma)\psi(0,t-s-u_0)$ in additive notation. Averaging over $u_0\in A_0$ gives zero unless $\psi\in\Psi(A_0)$, in which case $s\in A_0$ makes the remaining factor $\psi(\sigma)\psi(0,t)$ independent of $s$. Thus each surviving term has coefficient $mb|T_2|/|\Phi|=mb\delta_T/2$ after summing over the lifts; there is no factor $|A_0|$ left. Dividing [equation (4.5)](pdf#equation.4.5) by $|TT|mb\delta_T/2>0$ gives $G_{\mathcal K'}(x)-\Sigma_{\mathcal K'}(x)\le4x^{1/2+\varepsilon}+2x^{C\varepsilon}\mathrm{Br}/(|TT|mb\delta_T)+4/(x\delta_T)$.
apply-count-balance.Deduction.CharacterBalanceMoves.core: Fix $u_0$ and write $\mathrm{Th}(u_0,t)$ for the real part of the character sum with the thick weights replaced by $b$ and the thin terms set to zero. By the balance identity and the two bounds of `CostWindows`, $\mathrm{Th}(u_0,t)\le(\mathrm{ASK}-\operatorname{Re}\mathrm{MAIN})(a_t,t,w_{u_0,j})+2b/x$ for every lift $j$. The left side no longer depends on $j$, so summing this inequality over $t,j$ and using (3) gives $m\sum_{t\in TT}\mathrm{Th}(u_0,t)\le x^{C\varepsilon}\mathrm{Br}+2|TT|mb/x$ for each translate, before taking its mean over $A_0$.

average-kept-characters.Deduction.ch_core: For a kept character put $c_\psi=|TT|^{-1}\sum_{t\in TT}\psi(0,t)$. Since $\psi(\sigma)=1$, replacing the arguments $a_t/b$ by $x$ in the mean leaves $c_\psi G_\psi(x)$, with error $O(\log x)$ by (2) and the integrated derivative bound (only $O(1)$ for $\psi=1$). If $\psi$ is trivial on $H$ then $c_\psi=1$ exactly; otherwise $|c_\psi-\beta|\le Mx^{-1+\varepsilon}$, and the bound $|G_\psi(x)|\ll x\log x$ for non-trivial kept characters suffices to make the error in replacing $c_\psi$ by $\beta$ at most $O(x^\varepsilon\log x)$, with no square-root estimate assumed. For an omitted character the phase has modulus one, so the real mean is at least $-|G_\psi(x)|-O(\log x)$. As at most $M$ characters remain, these errors are $o(x^{1/2+\varepsilon})$ in total and the real mean is at least $G_{\mathcal K'}(x)-\Sigma_{\mathcal K'}(x)-4x^{1/2+\varepsilon}$.

analytic:141:1.Formalism.HC.HostRaw.ExceptionalCharacte: Among characters trivial on $H$ there are four sign characters, since $\mathfrak G/H=(\mathbb Z/2)^2$. Requiring also $\psi(\sigma)=1$ leaves two, the trivial character and the character `psC`; it excludes $\chi_\Phi$, which occurs in MAIN and takes the value $-1$ on $\sigma$. Both of the former have average one on $TT$, so keeping `psC` is possible only with the weight one assigned to a distinguished character of the level. In the levels `Level.cyc` used in the final proof there is no distinguished character: `ExceptionalCharacterKept` then requires `psC` to be omitted.

analytic:145:1.UpperTheory.Comparison₂.gmA_eq: At a prime power the inertia average gives the value of the inducing primitive Dirichlet character, even at primes ramified in the host; the centring term uses the logarithmic derivative of the same character, with the separate zeta term for the trivial one. To see the origin of the ordinary weight, `Shares` gives $A_0$ a share $4/(3o+1)$ of $TT$ and each of the other cosets a share $3/(3o+1)$, up to $x^{-1+\varepsilon}$ per share. For a non-trivial character of $H/A_0$ the equal shares cancel, leaving $1/(3o+1)$ at the identity coset. These are the weights of [(4.2)](pdf#equation.4.2) after the preceding weight-one cases are taken into account; `gmA_eq` identifies the two weighted sums exactly for every $y$, even though the host can change with $x$.

analytic:146:1.UpperTheory.Comparison₂.sigA_le: A character survives the translate average precisely when it descends to $(\mathbb Z/2)^2\times(H/A_0)$; this group has order $4o$, independently of the degree of the host. Of these characters one must bound both those with $\psi(\sigma)=-1$ and those with $\psi(\sigma)=1$ that are not in the level. For the hosts of the cyclic levels they are twists by at least one of the two new quadratic characters; [Statement 9.2](pdf#theorem.9.2) chooses the two primes so that these sums are small at $x$ (the prime powers in the sum run only to $x$, much less than the conductor of the twists). It makes no such assumption on the fixed characters one wants to treat.

analytic:148:1.UpperTheory.Comparison₂.core_gm: There are two contributions to the bound for the fixed level: with $C=e_D+e_L+3$, Statement 4.3 bounds $G_{\mathcal L}(x)$ by $x^{1/2+(e_D+e_L+6)\varepsilon}+4o\,x^{1/2+\varepsilon}$. Since $e_D+e_L\ge0$, the latter exponent is no larger than the former, and $o$ is fixed with the level; choosing $x$ large enough that $1+4o\le x^\varepsilon$ gives (4.6), with the $+7$ rather than $+6$. The threshold is independent of the host, but the inequality still requires the character hypotheses (`EAtH`) and the lattice hypotheses (`CoreAtH`) at the scale $x$.

analytic:155:1.Deduction.ch_top: Fix a translate $u_0$ and take the rank-weighted mean over its words $u$, not over the translates. The lattice inequality of [Section 5.6](pdf#subsection.5.6) compares the total count $\mathrm{ASK}(u_0)$ with the total main term $\mathrm{MAIN}(u_0)$; `IdentU` ties the sizes, weights and logarithmic derivative to those of the analytic identity, and `ch_top_main_eq` identifies the real main terms exactly. Hence the difference in (3), summed over $t,j$, is bounded by the lattice error, which `ch_top` bounds by a power of $x^\varepsilon$ times $\mathrm{Br}$. In `core_gm` the lattice data cover every $u_0\in A_0$, so one has this bound before taking the translate average in Statement 4.3.

analytic:158:1.Formalism.LFunctionChainParameters.Thick: The factor $m^2/k$ in the first term is a correction to the cost $x/m$: the lower bound $k\ge xm$ makes its contribution at most $2/\delta_T$. The upper bound on $k$ has a different purpose, to bound the third term; here the factor $|T_2|$ in the numerator cancels on division by $\delta_T=|T_2|/n$. Thus the second term pays both density losses, at most $2x^{\varepsilon/8}$ from $n/|TT|$ and $x^\varepsilon$ from $1/\delta_T$, while the third pays only the first. The rank interval must of course be nonempty: $xm\le n^2x^{1/2-\varepsilon}$, or $n^2\ge m x^{1/2+\varepsilon}$.

analytic:177:1.Formalism.LFunctionChainParameters.Thick: The leading part of the first bracket term is independent of $m$ for fixed $a_E,TT$; the second contains $m^2$. After division by $m$ their scales are $x/m$ and $m$, whose product is $x$: the model expression $x/m+m$ is least at $m=\sqrt{x}$, and the third cost is bounded separately by the upper bound on $k$. In the prescribed interval $x^{1/2-\varepsilon}\le m\le x^{1/2+\varepsilon/2}$ the largest exponent in the three upper bounds is $1/2+21\varepsilon/8$, from the second term: $\varepsilon/2$ from $m$, $\varepsilon$ from the explicit power, and $\varepsilon/8+\varepsilon$ from the two density factors. Division in [(4.5)](pdf#equation.4.5), with its factor $1/2$ and both additive errors retained, gives $G_{\mathcal K'}(x)-\Sigma_{\mathcal K'}(x)\le26x^{1/2+(C+21/8)\varepsilon}$; the condition $26\le x^{3\varepsilon/8}$ gives the stated exponent. This is the implication of `GrowthSizeBound`, proved by `proposition_size_bound`.

lattices:30:1.GlobalTheory.Mem.Col2.GStep.Fi: For a genus class $c$, let $V_c$ be the subspace of the complex weight representation fixed by the stabiliser of $c$ (with its character action). The choices of a value at different classes are independent, so `Fi` is the product of the $V_c$ and has dimension $\sum_c\dim V_c$. In particular, when the stabilisers are trivial, the rank of the integral lattice $M_u$ is the number of classes times the dimension of the weight representation. It is this full rank that is used in the choice of the level $T(u)$; a space cut out by prescribed Hecke eigenvalues would not have this dimension formula.

lattices:42:1.Formalism.BasicNotions.DV.Iu: Write $n_\lambda=\lfloor e_\lambda g(u,\lambda)\rfloor$. Locally the fractional ideal $I_u$ allows scalars of valuation at least $-n_\lambda$. With the infinite-place metrics unchanged, increasing $n_\lambda$ by one in a rank-$r$ lattice subtracts $r\log N\lambda$ from its log covolume, and hence adds $2\log N\lambda/[K:\mathbb Q]$ to its slope in the normalisation of Section 5.1. The rescaling is admissible because [Section 5.3](pdf#subsection.5.3) proves that the periods before rescaling have valuation at least $n_\lambda$ when nonzero; this also explains why a negative $n_\lambda$ is allowed.

lattices:42:2.Formalism.BasicNotions.DV.NprimeDef: There are two integral modules on the space of forms ramified at $T(u)$. The pullback of $M_u$ to that space is `MramL`; the module chosen before rescaling is `NuLat`. Away from $T(u)$, the latter is locally contained in the former, and agrees with it at dropped primes and at primes outside the inert and signal classes. If $L_u^0$ denotes `NuLat`, then `NprimeDef` says that the underlying module of $N_u$ is $I_uL_u^0$, the $\mathcal O_K$-span of all products of a scalar in $I_u$ and a form in $L_u^0$. Thus neither restriction to the ramified space alone nor multiplication of the whole $M_u$ by $I_u$ describes the lattice in (5.1).

lattices:42:3.Formalism.BasicNotions.SizeData₂.sg: For fixed $\lambda$ only the second correction $\mathrm{ee}_j(u,\lambda)$ depends on the word $u$. If the rational prime below $\lambda$ is dropped, `gainD` sets the gain to zero, not the two corrections. The ramification factor converts the sum of all $m$ contributions into the local valuation units; taking the negative floor then changes $-e_\lambda g(u,\lambda)$ by a number in $[0,1)$. Thus the rounding costs less than one valuation unit at each supported place, independently of the number of lifts, and there is no truncation at zero.

eleven-size-clauses.Formalism.LFunctionChainParameters.LChai: Fix $u_0$. The count $\mathrm{ASK}(u_0)$ and the gain $\mathrm{Ga}(u_0)$ are already single numbers; it is the slopes $\mu(N_u)-h(u)$, not the counts, that are averaged over $u$, with weights $\operatorname{rk}N_u$. The four displayed inequalities compare this mean with the common target slope $\mu(P)$ and the period bound. In the full record (Gain) also bounds $\mu_{\max}(N_u)$ from above, to control the error in (Slope), and (Loss) bounds the auxiliary index loss that enters $\mathrm{Lo}_5(u)$. The four closing clauses and the three positivity and size clauses make these comparisons effective at each translate, as required by condition (3) of [Statement 4.3](pdf#theorem.4.3).

lattices:65:1.Formalism.BasicNotions.SizeData₂.Ga: For a quantity $y$ in the units of $g(u,\lambda)$, the conversion to slope units is $2e_\lambda y\log N\lambda/[K:\mathbb Q]$ (`sz`). Over all places above a rational prime $p$ the coefficients of $y$ sum to $2\log p$, since $\log N\lambda=f_\lambda\log p$ and $\sum_{\lambda\mid p}e_\lambda f_\lambda=[K:\mathbb Q]$. This is the normalisation of the unramified-prime [count (4.3)](pdf#equation.4.3). The sum in $\mathrm{Ga}$ is over the finite support and deducts $\tau_\lambda$ once per place, after summing over the lifts: consequently $\mathrm{Ga}+\mathrm{Fo}-\mathrm{Ee}(u)=\sum_\lambda\mathrm{sz}_\lambda(g(u,\lambda)-\tau_\lambda)$ before rounding, with the further index losses accounted for in (Gain).

lattices:65:2.Formalism.BasicNotions.SizeData₂.Fo: The correction $\mathrm{Fo}$ is independent of $u$ at the fixed translate. Subtract (Div) from (Gain), writing $D(u)$ for the entire right side of (Div): one obtains $\mu(N_u)-h(u)-\mu(P)\ge\mu(M_u)+\mathrm{Ga}(u_0)-\mathrm{Ee}(u)-\mathrm{Lo}_5(u)-D(u)$. The height-adjusted slope on the left is precisely the quantity to be averaged in (Slope). The two occurrences of $\mathrm{Fo}$ have disappeared already, without any bound on their size.

lattices:65:3.Formalism.BasicNotions.SizeData₂.Ee: For each lift $j$, the finite-place sum of $\mathrm{ee}_j(u,\lambda)$ is compared with $\ell_g\sum_t a_t$, where $\ell_g$ is the logarithm of the product of the two fixed auxiliary level primes of the host, not the word-dependent prime $T(u)$. Adding the $m$ comparisons gives $\mathrm{Ee}(u)=m\ell_g\sum_t a_t$ up to $c_E mB_0$. The quantity to be controlled is the difference from this common leading term, not the absolute size of $\mathrm{Ee}(u)$, and the comparison holds for every word separately.

lattices:77:1.Formalism.RankGapBounds.WeightedMeanData: The lower bound for $\mu(M_u)$ goes into (Gain). To use [Statement 5.1](pdf#theorem.5.1) one must also control $u_F=\max_u(\mu_{\max}(N_u)-h(u))-\bar\mu$, the excess of the largest adjusted slope in the whole family over its mean. In comparing $\mu_{\max}(N_u)-h(u)$ with $\mu(N_{u'})-h(u')$, the upper and lower rescaling bounds cancel $\mathrm{Ga}$ and $\mathrm{Fo}$: what remains is the difference $\mu_{\max}(M_u)-\mu(M_{u'})$, the difference of $-\mathrm{Ee}-h$ between the two words, and the errors in rescaling. Taking the rank-weighted mean over $u'$ and then the maximum over $u$ gives the desired bound; this is why the maximal-slope bound in `Slopes` is needed as well as the mean-slope bound.

lattices:78:1.Formalism.RankGapBounds.WeightedMeanData: Put $A=\sum_t a_t$ and $H_u=h(u)+A\log T(u)$, where $h(u)$ is the chosen height bound. This is the height bound with the negative level contribution in (Div) added back. The clause `HComp` controls $|H_u-H_{u'}|$; to recover the variation of $h$ itself use $h(u)-h(u')=H_u-H_{u'}-A\log(T(u)/T(u'))$. The last inequality of `Count5` therefore gives an additional cost at most $Ac_{\mathrm{Count}}\log k$ in the comparison of adjusted slopes.

lattices:79:1.Formalism.LFunctionChainParameters.Weigh: For fixed $u_0$ the lower bound for $\log T(u)$ in `Count5` is independent of $u$, since the weights $w_j(\rho)$ are fixed. With $A=\sum_t a_t\ge0$, it gives an upper bound for the term $-A\log T(u)$ in (Div), in particular the term $-m\ell_g A$. The upper bound $\log T(u)\le c_{\mathrm{Count}}mL$ is needed instead in $\mathrm{Lo}_5(u)$, where the coefficient of $\log T(u)$ is $c_{\mathrm{Sl1}}|TT|m(a/k+b')$. Finally, the difference of the logarithms at two words is bounded by $c_{\mathrm{Count}}\log k$, so the estimate for $h(u)+A\log T(u)$ controls the variation of $h(u)$ as well.

lattices:79:2.Formalism.LFunctionChainParameters.Weigh: In the upper bound for the gain obtained by combining (Gain) and (Div), the level-dependent terms are $\mathrm{Ee}(u)-A\log T(u)$, with $A=\sum_t a_t$. Write $\mathrm{Ee}(u)=m\ell_gA+r(u)$ and the lower bound for $\log T(u)$ as $L_0+m\ell_g$, where $L_0$ is the weight term less the counting error. Then $\mathrm{Ee}(u)-A\log T(u)\le r(u)-AL_0$. [Statement 5.2](pdf#theorem.5.2) identifies the remaining period expression with the analytic main term plus the counting error, and `EComp5` bounds $|r(u)|$ by $c_E mB_0$; no smallness of $m\ell_g A$ is required. The same error bound gives $|\mathrm{Ee}(u)-\mathrm{Ee}(u')|\le2c_E mB_0$ in the estimate for $u_F$.

lattices:93:1.Formalism.MainNotions.LocalQuadraticPart: It is the period of the rescaled form that must be integral, not the form in the original lattice. Put $k_\lambda=\lfloor e_\lambda g(u,\lambda)\rfloor$; the period of an unscaled form belongs to $\mathfrak P_\lambda^{k_\lambda}$ locally, so multiplication by the factor $\mathfrak P_\lambda^{-k_\lambda}$ of [(5.1)](pdf#equation.5.1) leaves the pairing integral. The test vectors used at $\lambda$ give the pairings with the local generators of $R$; checking them at every finite place puts the image in $R^\vee=P$.

lattices:99:1.Formalism.L2.G.Adm2InU.admissible_level_: Away from $T(u)$ and the two host level primes, the last column of the lift is $cz$, with $z$ in the localised integral lattice and $v_\lambda(c)\ge e_\lambda(g(u,\lambda)+\Delta)$ when the period is nonzero. The period of $z$ has valuation at least $-e_\lambda\Delta$, where $\Delta$ is the denominator term `vDG`; the two terms in $\Delta$ cancel, giving the unrounded bound. At $T(u)$ the denominator term vanishes by coprimality, and at the two host primes the proof uses a separate bound and clears a local unit. The other conclusion of `admissible_level_two` applies off $T(u)$ to the larger ramified lattice before the orbit restrictions: the bound there has $\sum_j(\mathrm{fo}_j-\mathrm{ee}_j)$ in place of $g(u,\lambda)$, without the gain.

lattices:102:1.Formalism.MainNotions.G.gainP: On an orbit in $VV$ write $A_j=\max(g_0,0)$ and $\Delta_j=\max(g_U-\mathrm{Pr}-A_j,0)$ for lift $j$; its contribution is $A_j+\Delta_j$, and on the other orbits it is just $A_j$. In forming the local sublattice `NP` one may apply the orbit's Hecke operator $m$ times, or omit it and multiply by $p^{\lceil\sum_j\Delta_j\rceil}$ instead (`Sv`). The latter supplies the extra divisibility without the operator. The required gain and the compensation powers are the same for all words at fixed translate, sizes and weights; the lattices themselves and the correction $\mathrm{ee}_j(u,\lambda)$ in the exponent may change with the word.

lattices:111:1.Formalism.MainNotions.G.IsV: Write $n'=\operatorname{ord}(h_p)$ at a prime of the inert class. The dropped primes and the zero-gain case $h_p=0$ leave only cycles of even length, so an odd step $e$ changes the parity of the position $i$ measured from the base point. The parity also enters the local lattice model: `lamAt` uses the given weight at even positions and its negative in reverse order (the dual weight) at odd positions. In (5.2) it is the parity of the starting position, not the already odd exponent $e$, that determines whether a capacity is deducted in $g_U$.

lattices:116:1.Formalism.MainNotions.G.capU: The first copy contains the top places; the second contains the thick set of this local model. For odd $e$ the partner lies on the second copy at a prime of the signal class, and on the first at a prime of the inert class. If $w_j$ is the weight at that partner, the formula actually uses $c_t(e)=w_j-\mathrm{kaJ}(j)+c_G$ and $\alpha_t=a_t-2c_G$. Thus the weight tested against $\alpha_t/p^e$ is not the weight at $t$, nor exactly the weight in the analytic count.

lattices:123:1.Formalism.MainNotions.G.gU: Put $z=\alpha_t/p^e$ for an odd exponent. If it is not excluded, the extra contribution of $g_U$ over $g_0$ at an even position is $z-\max(z-c_t(e),0)=\min(z,c_t(e))$; at an odd position it is zero. An excluded exponent contributes nothing to $g_0$ but still contributes $z$ or $\max(z-c_t(e),0)$ to $g_U$, respectively. The common orbit correction cancels from this difference, whereas $\mathrm{Pr}$ is still to be paid; the rate $\gamma_p$ itself comes from the factorial valuation less the formal logarithm loss in [Section 6.1](pdf#subsection.6.1).

lattices:123:2.Formalism.MainNotions.G.g0: The uncorrected summand of $g_0$ has the positive-part form of the [count (4.3)](pdf#equation.4.3), but with $\alpha_t$ and $c_t(e)$ in place of $a_t$ and the partner weight, and with first arrivals omitted. These changes need not all decrease the summand: in particular the capacity is an adjusted weight. The inequality actually used in (Loss), in `LinkG_at`, bounds the count on the retained top places, summed over the lifts and less the error terms, by $\sum_j\mathrm{gain}_j(\lambda)-\tau_\lambda$; the other top places and primes are accounted for by the loss estimate. It is not a termwise equality between $g_0$ and the count.

lattices:126:1.Formalism.MainNotions.G.Excl: Suppose $t+h_p$ is another top place of an inert orbit of even length $n'$. The exponent $1$ is excluded, but $1+n'$ is not, although both are odd and have the same partner: only the least positive arrival at a different top place on the first copy is excluded. Consequently at an inert prime there is at most one excluded exponent per other top place of the orbit, while at a signal prime no odd exponent is excluded, since the partner is on the second copy.

lattices:132:1.Formalism.MainNotions.G.VV: At a candidate prime put $\sigma_p=m\sum_{t_0}\kappa_{t_0}$, the sum of `kapv` over the regular orbit representatives multiplied by the number of lifts. Either all these orbits enter $VV$, when $\sigma_p\le x^{-\epsilon}$, or none does. Besides the imposed restriction by $p^{\lceil\tau_p\rceil}$, the local index estimate has a further cost `ioP`, equal for nonempty $VV$ to $2\sigma_p\max_{t_0\in VV}\mathrm{Sv}(t_0)\le2x^{-\epsilon}\max_{t_0\in VV}\mathrm{Sv}(t_0)$; `LinkG_at` bounds the normalised colength off $T(u)$ by the rank times $\tau_\lambda+\mathrm{io}_\lambda$. It is $\tau_\lambda$ that is subtracted once in $\mathrm{Ga}$, not in the exponent $g(u,\lambda)$; the further index cost is controlled separately.

lattices:137:1.Formalism.MainNotions.G.Good: This is a condition on the set of positions, before the sizes and weights are chosen for the numerical test. In `IsGoodOrbit` the numbers of top places in cyclic windows of lengths $L_2$ and $G'$ are bounded by $K_G$ and $N_1$, respectively; in addition, divide the orbit from its base point into complete blocks of $(6r+1)U$ positions, with $U=\lceil1/\delta_1\rceil$ and $r=r_G$. From each block one finds, within the prescribed number of blocks (read cyclically), one whose odd-numbered cells of length $U$ are empty and whose even-numbered cells each contain exactly one top place, at an even position. This gives a run of $3r$ consecutive top places of even position, separated by more than $U$ steps; it does not require all top places of the orbit to be even.

st:F.Formalism.HN.TheoremF: The two frame bounds are used to compare ranks at one infinite place, not slopes. If a cut discards a fraction $r$ of the total source rank, let $U$ be the orthogonal complement of the span of the retained images in $W'_v$, put $z=\dim U/\dim W'_v$, and let $\operatorname{tr}_U Q$ be the trace of the compression of $Q$ to $U$. Only discarded source directions can contribute to this trace: the first bound, by Cauchy–Schwarz, gives $\operatorname{tr}_U Q/\operatorname{tr}Q\le(r+\sqrt{e_Fr})/(1-\sqrt{e_F})$, while the second gives $z-\sqrt{\eta_F z}\le\operatorname{tr}_U Q/\operatorname{tr}Q$ by subtracting the scalar part of $Q$. In particular, for $e_F=\eta_F=0$ one has $z\le r$; using $e_F\le1/4$ and $2\sqrt{\eta_F z}\le\eta_F+z$ gives $z\le\eta_F+4r+4\sqrt{e_F}$ in general. Projection onto the original rows of `Ball` (indexed by `Sum.inl`) cannot increase the absolute codimension; division by $\dim W_v\ge(1-\delta_F)\dim W'_v$ accounts for the enlargement factor. The ranks over $K$ can be read at $v$ in any bases, irrespective of the lattice metrics. [Section 7](pdf#section.7) supplies the frame bounds for the period maps.

rank-lost-at-a-filtration-cut.Formalism.HN.frameB_share: Count each slope $\lambda$ of $N_i$ with its rank multiplicity. Its deficit from the common upper bound, $\bar\mu+u_F-(\lambda-h_i)$, is non-negative, and the mean hypothesis bounds the sum of all these deficits by $u_F\sum_i\mathrm{rk}\,N_i$. Each slope cut away contributes more than $u_F+\tau$ to that sum, so the fraction cut away is at most $u_F/(u_F+\tau)$ for $u_F>0$; for $u_F=0$ all the adjusted slopes equal $\bar\mu$ and no rank is lost, even at $\tau=0$. Write $N_i(\tau)$ for the step retained at slope $\bar\mu-\tau+h_i$ (including equality). The minimum-slope inequality gives $\mu_{\min}(B_i(N_i(\tau)))\ge\mu_{\min}(N_i(\tau))-h_i\ge\bar\mu-\tau$ when the image is non-zero, so it lies in the step of $P$ of slope $\bar\mu-\tau$; the zero image lies there too. The frame estimate then bounds the rank of the sum of these images, which is a lower bound for the rank of that step of $P$.

lattices:204:1.Formalism.DivisorInequality.BoundsMu: The determinants here are ratios of Gram determinants. At the base type one needs the factorisation at every infinite place to take the mean of its logarithm; at a changed type the identity at $v_0$ suffices for the comparison of finite valuations, since the local Gram determinants are represented by field elements. Dividing by the common rank $D$ gives $\mu(R_{\mathrm{base}}^\vee)\le\operatorname{mean}_v\log\kappa_v-\sum_j\mu(M'_j)+\mathrm{Fo}+E$, where $E$ collects the remaining local terms, including the Hermitian discriminant contribution controlled in [Section 8.2](pdf#subsection.8.2). After passage to the level of $P$, the mean of $\log\kappa_v$ cancels against its negative in the height bound for $B_u$; thus it is the upper bounds on $-\mu(M'_j)$ that are needed in (Div).

lattices:208:1.GlobalTheory.BigTop.lamLow_of_hypotheses: On matching Hecke pieces the inner-product identities at the base embedding use the same $L$-values: for a single lift the scalar of $\theta_j\theta_j^*$ is $\lambda_j=c_jz_j$, and for the composite it is $c_0\prod_j z_j$. Their quotient is $\kappa=c_0/\prod_j c_j$. It is $\log\lambda_j$, not $\log\kappa$, for which the theorem supplies a lower bound: the $L$-value is in the region of absolute convergence, and the leading term of the bound is a sum of logarithms of hook products of weight diagrams. A hook product is at least the product of the factorials of its row lengths; the interlacing of the weights is what allows these factorials to account for all but the long top row in the kernel estimate, up to error.

lattices:220:1.Formalism.DivisionValues.divisor_inequal: For one lift $j$ and place $\rho$ the kernel estimate contains $\sum_i\operatorname{ph}(\nu_i)-n\log\Omega$, where $n=\sum_i\nu_i$ is its total degree (the squared norm contains the factor $\Omega^{-n}$). The degree identity is $n=a_\rho+kw_j(\rho)+\delta$, with $a_\rho$ put equal to zero off $TT$ for this calculation. In the full covolume term the coefficient of $w_j(\rho)\log\Omega$ is $p_j-q_j$, with $|p_j-q_j-k|\le m$; subtracting $n\log\Omega$ leaves $-a_\rho\log\Omega$ and the error $((p_j-q_j-k)w_j(\rho)-\delta)\log\Omega$. The factorial-minus-hook bound leaves at most $\operatorname{ph}(a_\rho)$ at a top place and zero elsewhere, up to error. Summing gives the factor $m$ on the surviving terms; the last map contributes $-\sum_t a_t\log T$ only once, as used in [Statement 5.2](pdf#theorem.5.2).

lattices:232:1.Formalism.L2.Pj.Core.cuspA: The space `cuspA` is over the coefficient field: it fixes the lift, weight and level, but imposes no integral structure. For a point $y$ above a finite place $\lambda$ the local norm of a nonzero evaluation is $(N\lambda)^{-v_y(f)}$, so the condition that it be at most one is exactly $v_y(f)\ge0$ (a zero evaluation also satisfies the condition). One takes the integral span of forms satisfying these tests everywhere, restricts to the specified type and takes the part selected by the idempotent. In coordinates this gives $M'_j$, the auxiliary lattice on the indefinite side, rather than the original lattice $M_u$ on the definite side.

lattices:233:1.GlobalTheory.CovTop.Assembly.lcv_le: Write $s_g,s_t,s_c$ for the slopes of the good, type and core lattices respectively, in the normalisation of the estimate, and $E\ge0$ for its unit of error. The good part has almost full rank, but this alone would not bound its slope: one also bounds the slopes that the small complementary part can carry. The resulting loss is at most $12e^{-x^{\varepsilon_z/7}}(x^A+x^B+C_1+C_2+1)E\le E$ for sufficiently large $x$, with the exponents and constants fixed. The four inequalities are then $\operatorname{lcv}(M'_j)/D\le-s_g$, $s_g\ge s_t-E$, $s_t\ge s_c-C_1E$ and $s_c\ge-\mathrm{mainT}_j-C_2E$; hence the normalised log covolume is at most $\mathrm{mainT}_j+(1+C_1+C_2)E$.

lattices:240:1.SelfIntersectionVolumeEstimates.topCovol: Below the top level the geometric argument passes to a deeper cover, where the height and arithmetic Hilbert–Samuel estimates give a lower slope bound for a space of sections. Multiplication by flat sections changes the weight: the degree of each relevant flat line has period contribution $(p'-q')\log\Omega/2$, and the multiplication changes the degree by minus the degrees of the sections used. The anchor comparison gives the main term $(p'-q')\sum_\tau\mathrm{anchor}_\tau\log\Omega$ in the slope normalisation, up to error; descent brings the lower slope bound to the core lattice. The theorem supplies the toroidal, Chow-height and small-section inputs to this construction and yields, through the preceding comparisons, the upper bound for the normalised log covolume of $M'_j$.

lattices:254:1.GlobalTheory.chowla_selberg_eta: The residue and constant term of $\zeta_K(s)=\zeta(s)L(s,\chi_d)$ at $1$ are $L(1,\chi_d)$ and $\gamma L(1,\chi_d)+L'(1,\chi_d)$, respectively. In Kronecker's limit formula the logarithm of the eta expression occurs with a minus sign; comparison of the constant terms thus gives the minus sign in (5.3). The mean logarithmic period in (Div) has a different normalisation, given by the metric of the CM generator: it is the class mean in (5.3) plus $\log(\sqrt d/(2v))$, hence $\log\Omega=\gamma+\log(\pi/v)-L'/L(1,\chi_d)$. The fixed field of $\Phi$ is $K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-d})$, so subtracting this period contributes $+a_tL'/L(1,\chi_\Phi)$ per top place and lift.

lattices:265:1.Formalism.MainNotions.StandardLattice.Cl: At one split place above $T$, $\mathrm{GL}_k(\mathbb F_T)$ acts transitively on the $T^k-1$ nonzero rows; the stabiliser of the chosen row therefore has this index. The product over the $f$ places gives the class-count factor. With trivial class stabilisers the rank of the space of forms is $d_u^*(T^k-1)^f$, where $d_u^*$ includes the mass, the index at the two host primes and the dimensions of the weight representations. The construction chooses $T(u)$ near $(D^*/(d_u^*\Gamma^2))^{1/(fk)}$ to make the source rank of order $D^*/\Gamma^2$ (where $D^*$ is the frame dimension parameter); estimating the logarithm of this ratio by the mass and Weyl dimension formulas is what supplies the lower bound below.

lattices:267:1.Formalism.LFunctionChainParameters.Weigh: Write $W_j=(\prod_{\rho\in\Phi} w_j(\rho))^{1/f}$ for the geometric mean of the weights of lift $j$. The displayed bound says that $T(u)\ge (v/\pi)^m\exp(m\ell_g)\prod_jW_j\,\exp(-cL_a(1+m^2/k))$, for every word at the fixed translate. The whole set of CM places enters the geometric mean, not just the thick or top places. Thus replacing $\log T(u)$ in the negative level term of (Div) gives precisely one mean of $\log w_j$ per lift, with the counting allowance added to the error.

st:key.Formalism.LFunctionChainParameters.Weigh: For one top place $t$ and one lift $j$, expand $\operatorname{ph}(a_t)=a_t\log a_t-a_t$ and combine the period and level terms. The expression $\operatorname{ph}(a_t)-a_t\log\Omega-\frac{a_t}{f}\sum_\rho\log(w_j(\rho)v/\pi)$ is exactly $a_t(\log a_t-1-\gamma+L'/L(1,\chi_\Phi)-\frac1f\sum_\rho\log w_j(\rho))$, the main term [(4.4)](pdf#equation.4.4). On summing over $t,j$ this accounts for every term except the host-prime correction and the counting allowance. The former is removed by the added $m\ell_g\sum_t a_t$ on the left of the identity; the latter is $+cL_a(1+m^2/k)\sum_t a_t$, since the lower bound for the level is subtracted only once, after the sum over lifts.

lattices:284:1.Formalism.LFunctionChainParameters.Weigh: Put $A=\sum_t a_t$. After Statement 5.2, (Div) bounds $\mu(P)+h(u)-\mathrm{Fo}$ by $\mathrm{MAIN}(u_0)-m\ell_gA$ plus errors. Inserting this in (Gain) leaves $m\ell_gA-\mathrm{Ee}(u)$ in the lower bound on $\mu(N_u)-h(u)$, so the upper inequality $\mathrm{Ee}(u)\le m\ell_gA+c_E mB_0$ is the one needed here. The main part is independent of the word, and the two-sided estimate also gives $|\mathrm{Ee}(u)-\mathrm{Ee}(u')|\le2c_E mB_0$ for the maximal-slope estimate. Both uses cost multiples of $mB_0$, already in the error budget; neither requires $m\ell_gA$ itself to be small.

lattices:298:1.Formalism.LFunctionChainParameters.Weigh: Fix $u_0$ and write $E_0$ for the four errors in `K0v5`, $E_F$ for the full error of (Slope) (including $\log|I|$), and $\overline{\mathrm{Lo}_5}$ for the rank-weighted mean of the losses. From (Gain), (Div) and Statement 5.2, with the bounds on the source slope and $\mathrm{Ee}$, one obtains $\mu(P)+\mathrm{Ga}(u_0)-\mathrm{MAIN}(u_0)-E_0-\overline{\mathrm{Lo}_5}\le\bar\mu\le\mu(P)+E_F$, the second inequality being (Slope). Thus (Loss) gives $\mathrm{ASK}(u_0)-\mathrm{MAIN}(u_0)\le E_0+E_F+\overline{\mathrm{Lo}_5}+\mathrm{Lo}$. The other loss bound, $\mathrm{IO}(u_0)\le\mathrm{Lo}$, bounds $\overline{\mathrm{Lo}_5}$ and hence helps bound $u_F$ in $E_F$; `each_unit_bound_statement` gathers these errors as `ErrX5at`. This argument averages over words, not translates: `ch_top` uses the further size and identification hypotheses to give the bracket bound at each $u_0$ required by [Statement 4.3](pdf#theorem.4.3).

divisibility:13:1.Formalism.L2.Th1.CM.ltLog: The first nonlinear coefficient is $1/\ell$, at degree $\ell^2$. Choose $\varpi$ with $\varpi^{\ell^2-1}=\ell$; the coefficient of $X^{\ell^{2j}}$ in $\varpi^{-1}\log_F(\varpi X)$ has valuation $1+\ell^2+\cdots+\ell^{2(j-1)}-j\ge0$ for $j\ge1$. cohomology:116:1.UpperTheory.V.Z.J.NumberU3U_s: Put $q=\mathrm N\lambda$. The finite trace list $(t_s)$ counts the rank-three cuspidal eigensystems and the rank-two newforms with a trivial summand adjoined, not merely their distinct numerical trace values. The product of $q^e(t_s-\mathrm{eis}(z_o))$ over $s,o$ is an integer because its factors are algebraic integers permuted by Galois, and is nonzero since the trace bound $|t_s|\le\sqrt q+2$ is less than $q^e-1-q^{-e}\le|\mathrm{eis}(z_o)|$ for $q\ge7$. Each factor has log absolute value at most $2e\log q+1$, and the cohomological dimension estimate bounds the number of indices by a polynomial in $N(e+1)$. At any coefficient prime $\ell\ne2,p$, the pairwise non-isomorphic admissible representations in each $X_o$ are assigned distinct indices (even when their traces coincide); $q^e$ is an $\ell$-adic unit and all unused factors are integral. Dropping those factors can only increase the absolute value of the product at $\ell$, giving the stated inequality.

cohomology:133:1.UpperTheory.V.Z.J.OneCharU_s: For a character $\psi$ in an orbit satisfying the hypotheses of Case I, write $L_\psi$ for its coefficient-ring length and $v_\ell$ for the valuation with $v_\ell(\ell)=1$. Use the preceding integer statement with a singleton (for each admissible representation) to obtain the trace non-equality at $\mathrm{Fr}_\lambda^{-1}$ required by `OneCharU_s`; the latter then gives finiteness and a bound for $V_n(\psi)=L_\psi/\operatorname{len}_{\mathcal O}(\mathcal O/\ell\mathcal O)$ by twice the sum of the trace-difference valuations in its finite family. Applying the integer statement to all these families at once and taking additive valuations gives $\sum_\psi V_n(\psi)\le2v_\ell(NN)$, so the sum weighted by $\log\ell$ costs at most $2\log|NN|$ for $\ell\ne2,p$; a second test prime covers $p$, and $2$ is treated separately. These Eisenstein congruences bound the character pieces of Sha; in [Statement 8.2](pdf#theorem.8.2) the lengths of Sha in turn bound the congruences between theta lifts and other eigensystems.

cohomology:137:1.UpperTheory.V.Alg.LemmaM: In the deformation problem of $r_0=\Psi\oplus1\oplus\Psi^{-1}$, conjugation by $\operatorname{diag}(u,1,u^{-1})$ grades the extension directions; the Selmer length is bounded by the length of the weight $-1$ cotangent module at the base point, modulo the equations of that weight. Set $a=\operatorname{tr}r(\sigma)-\operatorname{tr}r_0(\sigma)$ for the universal representation $r$: it has weight zero, vanishes at the base, and must be nonzero at each point that is neither upper nor lower triangular. The finiteness of the weight-zero algebra as an $\mathcal O$-module modulo the equations (`M2`) and the condition that there is at most one tangent direction at such a point (`M4`, the direction of the grading action) are part of the hypotheses of `LemmaM`. The conclusion is that finitely many orbits cover these points and the cotangent module has finite length, at most $2\sum_{\xi\in T}v(\xi(a))$ for any finite covering set $T$. Thus it is the integral size of the cotangent module at the base, not the dimension of the tangent space over the fraction field, that the trace differences bound.

cohomology:144:1.UpperTheory.V.Hi.hida_unitary_of_printed: The points whose traces enter the cotangent estimate are initially points of a Galois deformation problem; the trace list above, by contrast, is indexed by automorphic eigensystems. `hida_unitary_of_printed_hida` constructs an ideal $J$ of the ordinary determinant ring $B$ from unitary Hecke data; the ensuing `ModUAlt` gives $B/J$ finite over the weight algebra $\Lambda$, with the density and arithmetic-point properties. The argument propagates automorphy from seed points given by adjoint lifts of ordinary two-dimensional forms congruent to Eisenstein series. It is the later statement on the deformation problem that supplies finiteness and automorphy at the irreducible points and modularity of the two-dimensional pieces at the endoscopic points; the Hida statement alone is not an assertion of automorphy of every point.

cohomology:145:1.UpperTheory.V.Z.Kato.Final.zetaUr: For a representation attached to an $\ell$-ordinary newform of level prime to $\ell$, `zetaUr` supplies an integral class unramified away from $\ell$, lying outside the ordinary local condition at $\ell$, together with derivative data at auxiliary primes. At an eligible endoscopic point $W\oplus1$ the two off-diagonal pieces of the endomorphism representation are $W$ and $W^\vee\simeq W\otimes\theta$, since $\det W=\theta$ is quadratic. The consequence used here (`KatoTwoW`) is the vanishing of the Bloch–Kato Selmer groups for these two pieces, used with the other rigidity hypotheses to rule out extra tangent directions at the point. This is not the Euler-system estimate for the odd part above: here the numerical bound comes from the trace differences, and the Euler system supplies a condition for that bound.

cohomology:152:1.UpperTheory.Gal.Int.galoisRepresentation:
The geometric step starts in odd rank, with the cohomology of compact Shimura varieties: the Hecke–Frobenius relation constrains the Frobenius eigenvalues, and the genericity and weight-gap conditions serve to cut out a representation of the required dimension. Congruences and limits of traces remove the extra conditions on the forms of odd rank. For even rank $
u$, two lifts to odd rank $
u+t$ have at split unramified places the same twist of the original Satake parameter and two disjoint sets of added global characters $\{\psi_{1i}\}$ and $\{\psi_{2i}\}$. Writing $r_j$ for the Galois representation of the $j$-th lift and $\psi_{ji}$ also for its added $\ell$-adic characters, comparison at the split places identifies the two virtual representations $[r_j]-\sum_i[\psi_{ji}]$ ($j=1,2$); a negative multiplicity in their common value would require a character in both added sets, so this value is an actual semisimple representation. Undoing the twist, and using descent of the automorphic forms and patching over quadratic CM extensions, gives the assertion for $\mathrm{GL}_
u$; in [Statement 8.2](pdf#theorem.8.2) it is the eigensystems off the lift subset as well as those in it that need Galois representations.

cohomology:160:1.UpperTheory.GalStar.AwayB: At the split unramified places used in the congruence argument the equality given by `tor` supplies the Frobenius polynomials in `GoodR`. At the two auxiliary level primes, totally split and with $p>16\nu^2$, the condition called square-free permits a repeated eigenvalue of the tame generator if it is a $(p-1)$-st root of unity; in particular it permits the repeated eigenvalue of the character block. The clause `tame0` gives agreement of the inertia polynomials and also zero monodromy, without which a unipotent part of the inertia action could escape the polynomial comparison. In the application one obtains a polynomial $P$ over the Hecke algebra with $P_y(r_y(\gamma_0))(r_y(\gamma)-\chi_1(\gamma))=0$ at the eigensystems $y$, for inertia elements $\gamma$ and a tame generator $\gamma_0$; here $P_y$ is the specialisation at $y$, and $P_\pi(\chi_1(\gamma_0))$ is required to be a unit at the lift $\pi$. This is the relation used to make the relevant congruence cocycles unramified; equality of Frobenius actions at these ramified places is not needed.

cohomology:168:1.UpperTheory.TP.TLiftK: The threshold $n_0$ is chosen for the fixed good base datum and the source of rank $n_1$, with Hermitian matrix $1$; it precedes the choice of the target (of skew-Hermitian matrix $\delta\,1$), the form and the two splitting characters. At an infinite place $w$ of the real subfield, write $m_X(w),m_W(w)$ for the exponents of these characters. In the range $n_2\ge n_1$ the weight of the lift has $n_2-n_1$ entries equal to $(n_1+m_X(w))/2$; the other $n_1$ entries are this number plus $\lambda_{w,k}-(n_2+m_W(w))/2$, respectively, where $\lambda_w$ is the source weight. The hypothesis $n_2+m_W(w)\le2\lambda_{w,k}$ thus puts the first block at or above the added block. For the passage from even to odd rank one chooses a large odd $n_2$ and a splitting character of the prescribed restriction with $m_W(w)\le2\min_k\lambda_{w,k}-n_2$ at every $w$: it is not necessary to increase the weights of the original form.

cohomology:168:2.UpperTheory.TP.K.tLiftK: For a non-zero form $\phi$ and Schwartz datum $f$, the theta lift is $\int\theta_f(g,h)\overline{\phi(g)}\,dg$ over the source quotient. Write $c_\phi(g)=\langle R(g)\phi,\phi\rangle$ for the matrix coefficient of right translation and $C_f$ for the Weil coefficient in the Rallis formula: in the range $n_2\ge2n_1$, with $n_2/2$ larger than an integrability exponent of a height on the source group, it suffices to make $\int C_f(g)\overline{c_\phi(g)}\,dg$ non-zero. Schur orthogonality for the compact group at infinity gives a non-zero scalar factor, and the finite-place Schwartz data concentrate the Weil coefficient near the identity, where $c_\phi(1)=\|\phi\|^2>0$; a bound on the tail prevents cancellation. From the non-zero lift one takes an irreducible constituent, with the stated weights and the local theta pairings at split places. No non-vanishing of a special value of an $L$-function has to be established separately for this construction.

hosts:5:1.UpperTheory.Top.IsChiField: Let $E_0$ be the compositum of the real cyclotomic layer $\mathbb Q(\zeta_{2^{e_2+2}})^+$ and the field cut out by $\psi$ (the fixed field of its kernel in the cyclotomic field of its conductor). The first two tests say that the automorphism fixes $E_0$; the last two say that it fixes $\sqrt{-q}$ and $\sqrt{-d}$. Thus $E=E_0(\sqrt{-q},\sqrt{-d})$. The first two fields may intersect, but the two quadratic fields have distinct new prime conductors, prime to the conductor of $E_0$; consequently each contributes a separate sign to the Galois group, and every character of $E$ is a character of $E_0$ times a choice of the two quadratic characters.

quadratic-subfield-of-host.Formalism.HC.HostRaw: The quadratic field here is $K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-d})$ over $\mathbb Q$, not the maximal real subfield of $E$ or the quadratic extension of that real field. An embedding is in the CM type if it sends $\sqrt{-d}$ to $i\sqrt d$, and the stabiliser of this type is $\Phi=\ker\chi_\Phi$. For an unramified prime $p$ the sign on $\operatorname{Frob}_p^i$ is $(\frac{-d}{p})^i$, so the count selects just the odd powers at inert primes. The same choice of $K$ enters the mean of the CM period in [(5.3)](pdf#equation.5.3): its term $-L'/L(1,\chi_d)$ yields the term $+aL'/L(1,\chi_\Phi)$ in $\mathrm{MAIN}$ after multiplication by $-a$ in the period calculation.

hosts:18:1.UpperTheory.Top.WinPair: The congruences on $d$ are imposed so that every prime which may ramify in the host, except $d$ itself, splits in $K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-d})$. Indeed, $-d\equiv1\pmod p$ for $p=q$ and for every odd prime $p\le Y^{\varepsilon/5}$ (including the odd prime factors of the fixed conductor of $\psi$ for large $Y$), while $-d\equiv1\pmod8$ gives splitting at $2$. Hence at each of these primes the decomposition group of $E$ lies in $\operatorname{Gal}(E/K)=\Phi$: both inertia and any Frobenius representative lie in $\Phi$, though the prime need not split completely in $E$. At $d$ the new quadratic factor ramifies, and the inertia group has order two with nontrivial sign on $K$.

hosts:18:2.UpperTheory.Top.PageN: The real cyclotomic layer has degree $2^{e_2}$; adjoining the field of $\psi$ multiplies this by at most the order of $\psi$, and the two quadratic factors multiply it by four. In particular $n=|H|\asymp_\psi x^{2+8\varepsilon}$ when `PageN` holds. On a window $Y\le x\le Y^A$, the inequality $\log q/\log x>Y^{\varepsilon/5}/(2A\log Y)$ shows that the conductor exceeds every fixed power of $x$, while the degree grows only polynomially. Each new quadratic factor has degree two regardless of the size of its prime; it is the power-of-two layer that permits the degree to be adjusted at each scale.

st:supply.UpperTheory.Top.supplyChi: The exponent $401$ is the cutoff in the cohomological sum ($1\le e<t_0=\lfloor x^{401}\rfloor$); its bound controls a congruence index for the lifts in [Section 8.2](pdf#subsection.8.2). What is supplied in addition to that bound is a host adapted to the level of $\psi$, including the estimates for the auxiliary characters and the choice of the top places $TT$. Put $o=[H:A_0]$. The share of $TT$ in the zero coset of $H/A_0$ is approximately $4/(3o+1)$ and that in each of the other cosets is $3/(3o+1)$, with error at most $x^{-1+\varepsilon}$ in each share. For a nontrivial character of $H/A_0$ the sum over all cosets is zero, so the extra $1/(3o+1)$ on the zero coset leaves just the desired average $1/(3o+1)$, up to $o x^{-1+\varepsilon}$. This supplies the character weights in the reduction, without an assumption about the zeros of $L(s,\psi)$.

why-counts-windowed.UpperTheory.Top.supplyChi: At different scales the fields and their full character groups can differ, but the kept primitive characters and their weights give the same function $G_{\mathcal L}$ by `gmA_eq`. [Section 4.1](pdf#subsection.4.1) needs an upper bound on this one function throughout an interval: the integral against a concentrated Gamma kernel cannot be bounded from estimates only at isolated scales. If the construction needs the lower endpoint $W$ of the square window increased to $cW$ for a fixed $c\ge1$, the window $[cW,(cW)^{3/2}]$ still lies in $[W,W^2]$ for $W\ge c^3$.
why-counts-windowed.UpperTheory.Top.VWin: In `VWinAt` one fixes $\psi$, $\varepsilon$ and the layer function $e_2(x)$; then $J$ and a lower bound on $X$ are chosen, and the cohomological assertion must work for every admissible pair $(q,d)$ at $Y=X^{1/J}$. Thus the analytic prime choice can be made on the larger interval $[Y,Y^J]=[X^{1/J},X]$, using Statement 9.2 with $A=J$. Only then is the cohomological square window $[W,W^2]$ chosen inside it, for that same pair. The analytic estimates hold everywhere on the smaller interval, not merely at some points of it.

st:pairs.UpperTheory.Top.PairEx: After the average over the subgroup $A_0$ only characters of $(\mathbb Z/2)^2\times(H/A_0)$ occur. For the cyclic level of order $o$, the $o$ characters with neither quadratic twist are kept; the other three choices of $(i,j)$ account for the omitted sum, of at most $3o$ terms. The first two inequalities of Statement 9.2 are for the primitive characters inducing these twists, at $y$ throughout the chosen window, not for the fixed untwisted characters. The zero-box condition has a different purpose: the estimate at the thin places of [Section 4.3](pdf#subsection.4.3) concerns all host characters at $y\ge\exp(x^{\varepsilon/3})/3$; the new real characters are twists of real characters of modulus dividing $8M_0$, since a real character of the $2$-power units factors modulo $8$. Excluding their near-one real zeros permits the classical large-scale estimate; real characters without either new prime have bounded conductor.

estimates-for-auxiliary-twists.QH.meanSqK: Put $Z=Y^{400A}$ and $S_p(y)=\sum_{n\le Z}\Lambda(n)\min(1,y/n)\kappa(n)(\frac np)$, where $\kappa$ is fixed and $|\kappa|\le1$. The weight comes from [(4.1)](pdf#equation.4.1): replacing $L'/L(1,\chi)$ by its truncated negative prime sum leaves $-1$ for $n\le y$ and $-y/n$ for $y<n\le Z$, so $G_\chi(y)=-S_p(y)$ up to the logarithmic-derivative tail. On expanding $|S_p(y)|^2$, the character factor at $n,m$ is $(\frac{nm}{p})$; after removing square factors and the factors fixed by the progression, quadratic reciprocity reduces the nonconstant averages to sums of $(\frac ps)$ with odd squarefree $s\le Z^2$. The proof uses `twistK` to bound these except for one possible exceptional modulus, and bounds the remaining contributions separately, obtaining mean square $\le Cy\log y$. At a fixed $y$ the share with $|S_p(y)|>\tfrac12 y^{1/2+\varepsilon/2}$ is therefore at most $4Cy^{-\varepsilon}\log y$; a separate maximum estimate is needed to select one prime good for the whole window.
estimates-for-auxiliary-twists.Formalism.HermitianLattices.Ext.Primitiv: The zero-density estimate counts primitive characters having at least one zero in $\operatorname{Re}s>1-1/400$, $|\operatorname{Im}s|\le Q$, with conductor at most $Q$; there are at most $CQ^{1/4}$ such characters. Put $z=Y^{\varepsilon/5}$: for the first prime choice one may take $U=e^z$, $Q=8M_0U$, and for the second $U=\exp(z(\log Y)^2)$, $Q=8M_0e^z U=U^{1+o(1)}$. For each base character the varying new prime divides the primitive conductor, so distinct candidate primes give distinct primitive twists. Since there are only finitely many base characters (also with $q$ fixed in the second choice), the box can exclude only $O_{M_0}(U^{1/4+o(1)})$ of the at least $U^{9/10}$ candidates. On the remaining primes the logarithmic-derivative tail is controlled by the zero-free box, and the finite sum by the mean-square estimate.

hosts:63:1.Formalism.FrobeniusOrbits.ThickExists.no: Take the integer points $v$ of one squared norm in a box $[0,D)^s$, and map $v$ to $\sum_m v_m B^m$ with $B=4LD$. If three images satisfy the forbidden relation, the resulting signed digit at position $m$ is $j(v_{2,m}-v_{1,m})-i(v_{3,m}-v_{1,m})$, of absolute value at most $2L(D-1)<B$. Reduction modulo $B$ makes the first digit zero, and division by $B$ repeats the argument at every subsequent digit. The same relation then holds between the vectors, so three distinct points of the sphere would lie on a line, which is impossible.

hosts:64:1.Formalism.FrobeniusOrbits.hostThickExist: Let $N=|A_0|$, with generator $a_0$, and take $T_2$ to consist of the elements $sa_0$ for the integers $s$ supplied by `hostThickExists`. The condition $4Ls<N$ implies that a relation with coefficients $|i|,|j|\le L$ modulo $N$ is already an integer relation. Hence three visits within $L$ consecutive positions of an orbit of order greater than $4L$ are impossible: subtracting the first visit eliminates the translate, and eliminating the step gives the forbidden relation. An orbit of order $r\le4L$ cannot even meet the set in two distinct elements, for then $r(s_2-s_1)$ would be a nonzero multiple of $N$ of absolute value less than $N$. The bound $|T_2|\ge (N/L)\exp(-32\sqrt{\log N\log L})$ loses only a factor $x^{o(1)}$ for $N\asymp_\psi x^{2+8\varepsilon}$ and $L=O(\log x)$, leaving the density $\delta_T\ge x^{-\varepsilon}$ required in [Section 4.4](pdf#subsection.4.4).

offpath:71:2.Deduction.ch_core: In `GrowthInequalityForm` the average is over all of $H$ and the three non-trivial characters of $(\mathbb Z/2)^2$ must already have small sums at $x$, leaving an estimate for $G$ alone. Among these surviving characters one keeps a set $\mathcal K'$ of characters trivial on $\sigma$, with weight $1$ on those trivial on $H$ and $\beta$ on the others; the latter weight comes from the average on $TT$. offpath:75:1.Formalism.DworkPowerSeriesWeights.thmBGa: There are two copies of the variables in Theorem B. offpath:77:2.Formalism.B.DetGain: This is the prime-factorisation argument for a single non-zero integer $\Delta$. If $p\nmid\Delta$, the condition forces $g_p\le0$; for primes dividing $\Delta$ the full budget is $\sum_p v_p(\Delta)\log p=\log|\Delta|$. Hence summing $g_p\log p$ over any specified finite set of primes costs at most this budget, without requiring $g_p\ge0$. The same elementary device explains the utility of one integer for all coefficient primes in the cohomological bounds below, but this particular proposition is outside the cone.
